Summarize the following incident postmortem.

---

Incident: customer-facing API returned TLS errors for 47 minutes on 9 April.

At 06:12 UTC the public API began rejecting connections with certificate errors. The root cause was an expired TLS certificate on the regional load balancer. The certificate had been issued manually two years earlier, outside the automated renewal pipeline that covers every other endpoint, because the load balancer was provisioned during an emergency migration and never moved into the infrastructure-as-code repository.

Detection was slow. Our synthetic monitoring checked the API only from inside the private network, where traffic reaches the service through an internal endpoint that uses a different certificate. The first signal came from customer support tickets at 06:31 UTC, nineteen minutes after impact began. The on-call engineer confirmed the expiry at 06:44 UTC, issued a replacement certificate through the automated pipeline, and attached it to the load balancer. Error rates returned to normal at 06:59 UTC.

Impact: roughly 38 percent of API requests failed during the window. Mobile clients retried aggressively, which tripled request volume and briefly raised latency on unaffected regions once service recovered. No data was lost.

What went well: the automated pipeline issued a valid certificate in under five minutes once engaged, and the incident channel stayed focused.

Action items: import the load balancer into the infrastructure-as-code repository so its certificate joins automated renewal; add external synthetic monitoring that exercises the public endpoint and alerts on certificate expiry thirty days ahead; add jittered exponential backoff to the mobile client retry policy; audit all endpoints for manually issued certificates.

Summarize the following technical passage about the Raft consensus algorithm.

---

Raft is a consensus algorithm designed to be easier to understand than Paxos while providing the same safety guarantees. A Raft cluster typically has an odd number of servers, such as three or five, so that a majority, called a quorum, can always be formed while tolerating the failure of a minority of nodes.

At any time each server is a follower, a candidate, or the leader. Followers are passive: they respond to requests from the leader and from candidates. If a follower receives no heartbeat from a leader within its election timeout, it becomes a candidate, increments the current term, votes for itself, and asks the other servers for votes. Election timeouts are randomized, typically between 150 and 300 milliseconds, which makes split votes rare. A candidate that collects votes from a majority becomes leader for that term.

The leader handles all client writes. It appends each command to its log and sends AppendEntries messages to followers, a process called log replication. Once an entry is stored on a majority of servers it is committed, and the leader applies it to its state machine and reports success to the client. Followers apply committed entries in the same order, so every server's state machine passes through the same sequence of states.

Safety rests on the election restriction: a candidate cannot win unless its log is at least as up to date as the logs of a majority of voters. This guarantees that a newly elected leader already holds every committed entry, so committed data is never lost when leadership changes.

In practice, clusters must also handle membership changes and log growth. Raft uses joint consensus or single-server changes to add and remove members safely, and periodic snapshots to compact the log. Raft underpins widely used systems such as etcd and Consul. Its main costs are write latency, since every commit needs a round trip to a quorum, and reduced availability when a majority of nodes is unreachable.

Summarize the following explainer about residential heat pumps.

---

A heat pump heats a home by moving heat rather than generating it. In heating mode it absorbs heat from outdoor air, even cold air, using a refrigerant that evaporates at low temperature. A compressor raises the pressure and temperature of the refrigerant vapor, and an indoor coil releases that heat into the house. Running the cycle in reverse provides air conditioning in summer.

Efficiency is measured by the coefficient of performance, the ratio of heat delivered to electricity consumed. A modern air-source unit typically achieves a coefficient of performance between 2.5 and 4 in mild weather, meaning it delivers two and a half to four units of heat for each unit of electricity. Electric resistance heating, by comparison, has a coefficient of exactly 1. Efficiency falls as the outdoor temperature drops, because there is less heat to extract and the compressor works harder.

Older heat pumps struggled below freezing, which earned them a reputation as unsuitable for cold climates. Cold-climate models with variable-speed inverter compressors now keep producing useful heat down to about minus 25 degrees Celsius, although many installations still keep a backup heat source for the coldest days.

Homes with existing ducts can use a central ducted unit. Homes without ducts often use ductless mini-split systems, with one outdoor unit serving several wall-mounted indoor heads, which also allows room-by-room temperature control.

The main barrier is installation cost, which is usually higher than replacing a gas furnace. Operating savings depend on local electricity and gas prices; where electricity is cheap relative to gas, payback can take under ten years, while elsewhere it may never pay back on cost alone. Rebates and tax credits in many countries narrow the gap. Proper sizing and installation matter as much as the equipment: an oversized unit cycles on and off frequently, reducing efficiency and comfort.
